source.title: Evidence of a log scaling law for political persuasion with large language models
source.authors: Kobi Hackenburg; Ben M. Tappin; Paul Röttger; Scott A. Hale; Jonathan Bright; Helen Margetts

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether model scale predicts a downstream outcome, political persuasion, using human survey treatment effects rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The study measures political persuasion of generated messages across model sizes. It does not test held-out cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its introductory references to pretraining loss and other scaling results are cited background, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures how a downstream outcome, human attitude change from LLM-written political messages, varies with model size across 24 models from 70M to over 300B parameters. That bears on V6 in a new, human-evaluated setting. It reports nothing on pretraining loss, compute allocation or architecture shape (V1–V5, V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report a log scaling law with sharply diminishing returns: frontier models are barely more persuasive than models an order of magnitude or more smaller. Task completion (coherence, staying on topic) appears to account for larger models' advantage, a mediation inference they say should be held lightly. They conclude that further scaling will not much increase the persuasiveness of static LLM-generated messages.
record.recipe_differences: The study estimates human attitude change from generated political messages in a randomized survey, rather than measuring held-out language-model loss or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The size association varied across political issues. It was robust to a model-family fixed effect and to alternative assumed sizes for the frontier models; it was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for task completion.
record.code_released: Code and replication materials are publicly available in the project GitHub repository; URL not stated.
record.problems: Model sizes for GPT-4-Turbo and Claude-3-Opus are unknown and assumed; participants skewed liberal, Democratic, and female; the authors caution that the task-completion mediation interpretation is observational and should be treated cautiously. Several robustness results are only summarized in text and their cited supplementary tables are not included.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. Individual model estimates in Figure 1 are recorded as figure-only because the main text does not give their values separately.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss rather than parameter count; other downstream tasks; forecasting the outcome of larger, future models from smaller ones; multi-turn or personalised persuasion.

missing.what: Task completion score rises strongly and nonlinearly with model size; frontier models score the maximum of 3.
Estimated persuasiveness ceiling of about 12 pp in aggregate across issues.
The result is robust to assumed frontier sizes up to and beyond 1T parameters.
missing.locator: Results; Fig. 1 caption; Supplementary Fig. S4

missing.what: No model is significantly more persuasive than the human benchmark messages.

record.verdict_notes: The 'log scaling law' is linear in log(parameters) on a treatment-effect scale. It is not a power law in loss, so it speaks only to V6 as a downstream regularity. The sizes of the two frontier models are assumed, not known. The open models were all fine-tuned the same way on GPT-4 Alpaca, while the closed models were not. Size is confounded with model family and recipe, though a family fixed effect was tested. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens, and how either grows with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling laws in other modalities and training regimes, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Other downstream tasks, and predictability from pretraining loss rather than model size.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents and compute-optimal allocation on the listed setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: 24 language models (aggregate random-effects meta-analysis)
rows.size_stated: Open-weight models: 70M to 72B parameters; GPT-4-Turbo and Claude-3-Opus sizes unknown and assumed to be at least 300B for the primary analysis.
rows.stage_stated: Open-weight base models fine-tuned on the same instruction-following data; the two closed-source model systems were also tested.
rows.operation_detail: Estimated the association between model parameter count and message persuasive impact in a randomized survey experiment.

conditions.value: 30 per model; three per issue across 10 issues
Treatment effect relative to no-message control

rows.measure: Change in persuasive impact associated with a one-unit increase in the natural logarithm of parameter count
rows.baseline: No-message control; the coefficient is a change in estimated treatment effect, not an absolute treatment effect.
rows.value: 1.26 percentage points; estimated average treatment effect at the sample’s average model size (37.9B parameters) was 5.77 percentage points.
rows.uncertainty: 95% CI for log(parameter count) coefficient [0.65, 1.87], p < 0.001; 95% CI for intercept [4.07, 7.48].
rows.note: The authors describe the association as logarithmic with sharply diminishing returns. The meta-analysis pools message, model, and issue variation.

rows.subject: 24 language models (aggregate analysis adjusted for task completion)
rows.size_stated: Open-weight models: 70M to 72B parameters; closed-source model sizes unknown.
rows.stage_stated: Open-weight base models fine-tuned on the same instruction-following data; closed-source systems also tested.
rows.operation_detail: Re-estimated the model-size association with task completion score included as an adjustment.
rows.measure: Association between log parameter count and persuasive impact conditional on task completion
rows.baseline: Unadjusted size coefficient was 1.26 percentage points per one-unit increase in log parameter count.
rows.value: The association shrank toward zero and was no longer statistically significant; no adjusted coefficient is stated in the main text.
rows.locator: Results, Figure 3D and accompanying text; Supplementary Information Table S5 cited but not included
rows.note: The authors say task completion remained a statistically significant predictor in the adjusted analysis.
rows.check: This is an observational mediation analysis, not a test of whether scale predicts the outcome. The adjusted coefficient is only plotted (Fig. 3D) and its table (S5) is not in the text.

rows.subject: 24 language models (pre-training-token comparison)
rows.stage_stated: Open-weight base models fine-tuned on the same instruction-following data; closed-source systems also tested.
rows.operation_detail: Compared pre-training token count with parameter count as predictors of persuasive impact.
rows.measure: Predictiveness of pre-training token count for model persuasiveness
rows.baseline: Parameter count used as the alternative scale measure; numerical comparison not stated.
rows.value: Pre-training token count was far less predictive of model persuasiveness.
rows.locator: Methods 4.1; Results, Figure 3A and accompanying text
rows.note: No numerical effect estimate for the token-count comparison is supplied in the main text.
rows.check: Fig. 3A and Methods 4.1 show pre-training token count is not a significant predictor; only task completion is. So size measured in tokens shows no effect, not a partial one.

rows.subject: 24 language models (issue-level random-effects estimates)
rows.size_stated: Open-weight models: 70M to 72B parameters; closed-source model sizes unknown.
rows.stage_stated: Open-weight base models fine-tuned on the same instruction-following data; closed-source systems also tested.
rows.operation_detail: Estimated variation across political issues in the model-size association with persuasive impact.
rows.measure: Between-issue standard deviation of the log parameter-count association
rows.baseline: Mean association across issues; numeric mean slope not separately stated here.
rows.note: The authors describe diminishing returns as sharper on some issues and less sharp on others; issue-specific slopes are shown graphically.

rows.subject: 24 language models (analysis with model-family fixed effects)
rows.size_stated: Open-weight models: 70M to 72B parameters; closed-source model sizes unknown.
rows.stage_stated: Open-weight base models fine-tuned on the same instruction-following data; closed-source systems also tested.
rows.operation_detail: Re-estimated the model-size association with a fixed effect for model family.
rows.measure: Robustness of the model-size association with persuasive impact
rows.baseline: Primary meta-analysis without the family fixed effect.
rows.value: The key result remained robust; a numerical coefficient is not stated in the main text.
rows.locator: Results; Supplementary Information Table S4 cited but not included
rows.note: The supplementary table is not part of the provided text.

rows.subject: 24 language models (nonlinear-form robustness analyses)
rows.size_stated: Open-weight models: 70M to 72B parameters; closed-source model sizes unknown.
rows.stage_stated: Open-weight base models fine-tuned on the same instruction-following data; closed-source systems also tested.
rows.operation_detail: Added quadratic or cubic terms for log parameter count to the linear meta-analysis.

conditions.value: Quadratic and cubic terms tested separately

rows.measure: Whether nonlinear terms predict persuasive impact beyond the linear log-size term
rows.value: Neither quadratic nor cubic terms significantly predicted persuasiveness beyond the linear term.
rows.locator: Results; Supplementary Information Table S3 cited but not included
rows.note: This supports the linear-log form in the tested setting; exact coefficients and significance values are not in the provided text.

relationships.condition: Aggregate across 24 models, static political messages, size measured as parameter count
relationships.reason: Persuasiveness rises 1.26 pp per log-parameter unit (CI 0.65–1.87) (R1). Quadratic and cubic terms add nothing beyond the linear-log term (R6). The result holds with a model-family fixed effect (R5).
relationships.display_finding: Persuasiveness rose 1.26 percentage points per log-parameter unit, with a confidence interval of 0.65–1.87; higher-order terms added no explanatory value, and the relationship held after adjusting for family.

relationships.reason: Returns diminish sharply. Qwen1.5-7B and Llama-2-13B are not significantly less persuasive than frontier models (R7, R8), and authors estimate a ceiling near 12 pp.
relationships.display_finding: Qwen1.5-7B and Llama-2-13B were not significantly less persuasive than frontier models, and the estimated ceiling was near 12 percentage points.

relationships.condition: Choice of scale measure and adjustment for task completion
relationships.reason: Pre-training token count does not predict persuasiveness (R3). The size effect becomes non-significant once task completion is adjusted for (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Pretraining-token volume did not predict persuasiveness, and the parameter-size effect became nonsignificant after adjusting for task completion.

relationships.reason: The slope on log parameter count varies by issue (SD 0.87 pp against a mean of 1.26) (R4).
relationships.display_finding: The slope against log parameter size varied across issues, with a standard deviation of 0.87 percentage points against a mean of 1.26.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Aggregate model-size sweep for static political messages in the tested survey setting
reader_labels.reason: Persuasive impact increased with log parameter count; the estimated coefficient was 1.26 percentage points per log unit (R1), and added quadratic or cubic terms did not significantly improve the linear-log fit (R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across political issues and after adjustment for task completion
reader_labels.reason: The size association varied by issue (R4), and it was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for task completion (R2); the result concerns static political messages and does not establish general downstream-task predictability.
